content: Widely available routine data should focus on essential figures that summarize program performance and describe basic aspects of data quality. A minimalistic approach, concentrating on a few key indicators with appropriate disaggregation, can be highly effective. Ideally, platforms generating these displays should allow managers to interact with the data, enabling further exploration of unexpected results. This includes assessing whether poor data quality contributes to anomalies or whether the results genuinely reflect program performance. Such tools can serve as the focal point for routine cascade data review meetings or, at the very least, provide standardized analytic outputs for decision-making. Materials for routine analysis include a subset of 11 program cascade indicators (selected from 15 national core indicators) with recommended data dashboards, explanations for their use and interpretation, and training exercises to help interpret dashboard figures using program data. These resources are detailed in the Analysis and Use of Health Facility Data: Guidance for HIV Programme Managers document. The HIV cascade dashboard provides a cross-sectional view of the percentages of people living with HIV who are diagnosed, linked to treatment, and have achieved viral suppression. This analysis is conducted at both national and subnational levels, as well as for priority populations. In 2018, WHO and partners published the Cascade Data Use Manual, which includes examples of cascade analysis using various data types for different program management purposes. These examples cover HIV treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services for mother-infant pairs, and patient groups with HIV and co-morbidities such as tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. The cascade analysis approach can also be applied to prevention contexts, tracking both HIV-positive and HIV-negative members of high-risk groups, including key populations. The manual outlines key steps for conducting and using data from cascade analyses, including assessing data quality, identifying gaps, and applying strategies to address common gaps in the cascade. Cascade analyses based on aggregate data have limitations, particularly in countries with low service coverage. However, these figures can still provide valuable insights into comparative gaps in service access. Countries with individual-level health information systems (HIS) and unique identification standards (UIS) can perform robust cascade analyses, as these systems allow for deduplication. When electronic HIS and UIS extend to include HIV testing services, more comprehensive cascade analyses can be conducted, including linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART). In the absence of such electronic tools, countries must establish more complex mechanisms for tracking individuals through paper-based systems designed for cohort analysis. Countries should periodically employ data triangulation methods to compare and integrate data from different sources to corroborate the interpretation of core cascade analysis results. Examples of additional data sources include special survey data and qualitative information from service providers and clients. Routine data review can also be expanded to inform specific program improvements. Quality improvement (QI) is a systematic approach to enhancing program performance as part of a routine process. QI involves measuring performance using standardized indicators, identifying quality challenges, exploring root causes, designing and implementing contextually appropriate solutions, and assessing their impact through rapid, iterative tests of change. Many HIV programs use QI methods tailored to local capacity, resources, and data availability. The Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle is a commonly used QI method. Regardless of the model used, HIV programs should institutionalize a culture and capacity for improvement across all levels, including routine cascade data review activities. QI requires quality data collection, reporting, and use of indicators, typically focusing on a subset of high-priority service indicators and disaggregated cascade analyses. Interoperable information systems facilitate measuring service quality, addressing knowledge gaps, and communicating findings to end-users such as district health management teams and facility-level quality committees. The emergence of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) is a global concern, threatening the effectiveness of ART and sustained reductions in HIV-related morbidity, mortality, and transmission risk. WHO's 2019 global report on HIVDR documented increasing levels of NNRTI resistance, exceeding 10% among adults initiating first-line ART in most monitored countries. High levels of NRTI resistance have also been observed in infants newly diagnosed with HIV and in individuals failing ART. The introduction of dolutegravir (DTG), an integrase inhibitor, has mitigated the trend of NNRTI pretreatment resistance. However, ongoing surveillance and efforts to prevent the emergence and transmission of HIVDR remain a priority. WHO recommends integrating actions to prevent, monitor, and respond to HIVDR into every national HIV program, including routine cascade data reviews. Data from various sources enable stakeholders to identify programmatic and epidemiologic evidence of the need to strengthen relevant program services and potentially revise ART guidelines. Routine data reviews are most effective when implemented as a system with supportive governance and organizational structures to engage managers and partners. The first step is to convene the right group of individuals for routine data review, defining their roles and responsibilities for analysis, interpretation, documentation, and follow-up, and setting a schedule for review meetings. The frequency of data review should correspond to the management level, with facility managers reviewing data more frequently (e.g., weekly or monthly) and national managers less frequently (e.g., quarterly or semi-annually). Including all relevant partners in data review discussions ensures that outputs and decisions are fully acted upon. Hybrid technical groups comprising programmatic, technical, and data experts are critical for effective convening. The second step is to develop a plan for standard core analysis, specifying priority indicators, disaggregations, and analytic outputs. Participants in routine data review meetings should receive data in a standard format and be trained in its use and interpretation. The third step is to translate discussions on core analysis interpretation into actionable steps for managers. Findings and action plans developed at one level may inform actions at other levels. Documenting actionable next steps, responsible persons, and timelines ensures accountability and coordination across management levels. Routine data meetings should review past action plans and compare current service delivery to past trends to assess the impact of previous actions. This cyclical approach aligns with a continuous QI process informed by data. Electronic health information systems (HIS) play a crucial role in collecting, organizing, analyzing, and reporting data for programmatic decision-making. Primary data collection tools must capture necessary data elements in a format that facilitates patient care, paper-based aggregation, or individual-level data entry. In resource-poor settings, data entered into electronic HIS should reflect relevant data use cases, including patient care, program management, and monitoring. WHO has developed supplemental materials to facilitate the incorporation of WHO standards into digital systems. To optimize program management based on routine data reviews, countries should adopt interoperable data platforms across all geographic areas and health facility levels. Funders should support systems that comply with public health sector standards and multisectoral digital authorities. Governance over HIS policies and standards should be established by the ministry of health or equivalent entities.
